message:
# XChem lab design with synchrotron diffraction kept external

**I haven't added an in-house X-ray diffractometer.** In this setup, fragment data collection has to stay an external synchrotron step, with shipping and beamline queue time kept in the model. I also found no evidence for how a home X-ray source would perform on fragment datasets, so I couldn't model one honestly. What follows is the best provisional design I can give without your input.

## My assumptions (none of these came from you)
- **Target:** 50 successful harvested crystals per day. That means 2 crystallisation plates per protein batch, 32 attempted crystal mounts per plate, and 2 sixteen-crystal pucks per plate.
- **Mount success:** 86%, from Wright et al. 2021, so about 27.5 successful crystals per plate. Failed mounts are not counted. "Successful" means the mount was judged good, not that the crystal diffracted well or bound a fragment.
- **Room:** 10 m × 7 m with one door.
- **Budget:** none given, so this is provisional.
- **Staff:** one protein scientist and one crystallographer, each on an 8-hour day shift. Instruments can run unattended overnight.
- **Hazards:** liquid nitrogen, so the cryogen area needs ventilation and oxygen monitoring. Biosafety level 1 for the expression work. The drop-setting robot and the imager are placed in vibration-free zones.
- **Estimated times (not from sources):** crystal growth takes 3 days (range 1–14). Soaking takes 2 hours (range 0.5–24). Loading pucks into the dry shipper takes 900 s per plate's 2 pucks (range 300–3600). This is handling time, not how long the shipper holds its cold.
- **Synchrotron:** shipping plus queue is 7 days (range 2–21 days), a placeholder from the catalog. Beamline collection is about 2,304 s per puck (catalog estimate). The dry shipper (`shipper_1`) is referenced inside this shipping step.
- **Imaging:** each inspection takes 3 minutes per plate on a single camera, at day 0 and before drop selection. Inspections in between are not modelled.
- **Growth storage:** the imager's 1,000-plate hotel can't be modelled separately from its single camera. So growth time is modelled in a Cytomat incubator (42 slots) instead.

## Harvesting time, from the Wright et al. 2021 comparison
- **With the Shifter:** an average of 35 s per attempted mount (range 15–36 s). For 32 mounts that's 1,120 s per plate (range 480–1,152 s). An operator is present the whole time.
- **Fully manual (no Shifter):** about 8 crystals per hour, so the same 32 mounts would take about 4 hours per plate.

## Equipment (about $981k, catalog estimates only)
| Stage | Equipment |
|---|---|
| Protein production | Multitron shaker, Avanti centrifuge, EmulsiFlex lyser, ÄKTA pure 25 purifier, Mini-PROTEAN gel system, NanoDrop |
| Crystallisation | mosquito Xtal3 drop setter on a vibration table, Rock Imager 1000, Cytomat 2 incubator |
| Soaking | Echo 525 acoustic dispenser |
| Harvesting and shipping | Crystal Shifter, handling bench, LN2 dewar, CX100 dry shipper |

The Rock Imager (about $350k) and the Echo (about $246k) make up most of the cost. The total excludes installation, service and consumables.

## Results (model predictions, not measured performance)
- **Throughput in the planning simulation:** median 151.4 crystals per day. The pessimistic case (P10) is 89.7 and the optimistic case (P90) is 206.4. The probability of reaching 50 per day was 1.0 under these assumptions.
- **Independent check:** the verifier re-ran the model and got a lower median of 114.7 and a pessimistic case of 93.8 crystals per day. Both runs clear the assumed target. The planning number has not been independently confirmed, so use the lower figure.
- **Layout:** no violations.
- **Where the time goes:** the incubator is the busiest instrument, used 75% of the time, mostly because of the 3-day growth step. Growth time has the biggest effect on throughput in the model. The crystallographer is busy 56% of the time. The simulator may not fully apply 8-hour shifts, so that figure could be optimistic.
- **The wait you're worried about:** one batch takes about 483 hours (roughly 20 days) from expression to analysis. About 169 hours of that is the external shipping and beamline step, and no layout change can shorten it.

## What this means for waiting on beamtime
This design keeps pucks flowing so that daily output stays high. It does **not** shorten the time from one crystal to its dataset. The practical options are:
- send shipments on a regular schedule (each plate fills 2 pucks), so harvesting continues while samples wait in the queue;
- book beamtime early;
- treat the 2–21 day turnaround as a range when planning.

I didn't make further changes because the design already meets the assumed target. The report's caveats apply: every number depends on placeholder assumptions about protein yield, growth time, soak time and queue time.

first_reply:
I can't add an in-house diffractometer to this XChem design. In this planning setup, fragment diffraction is fixed as an external synchrotron step, and the shipping and beamline queue time has to stay in the model. I won't put a local X-ray instrument into the equipment list or workflow, and I won't remove the queue time to make the schedule look faster.

There's also a practical reason not to model it: fragment screening usually depends on high-flux beamlines and fast automated data collection. I haven't retrieved any evidence on how a home-source diffractometer would perform for fragment datasets, so any throughput number I gave you would be made up.

**What I can do about the wait:**
1. **Model the synchrotron wait honestly.** I'd keep shipping and beamline queue time as a separate, uncertain value (using your typical turnaround if you have it). The simulation would then show how much of the total time is that wait and how much is lab work.
2. **Make sure the in-house work isn't what's slowing you down.** Expression, purification, drop setup, growth and imaging, soaking, manual harvesting, and puck loading into the dry shipper would all be sized so each shipment has full pucks ready. I can also test whether something like a second Shifter or more operators would raise crystals per day.
3. **Plan shipments around beamtime.** If you have recurring beamtime slots, I can set the number of pucks per shipment and how often you ship, so that queue time overlaps with your crystal production rather than adding to it.

**To build and simulate this, I need:**
- **Target throughput:** a number and unit, such as harvested crystals per day or per week. Please also say whether you count attempted mounts or only successful crystals.
- **Room size:** width × depth in metres, plus door locations and any areas where equipment can't go.
- **Budget** in USD. If you don't have one yet, you can let me make a provisional design without it.
- **Operating hours per day and operators:** how many people, their roles, and shift lengths. Harvesting needs an operator for the whole step.
- **Hazards and constraints:** liquid nitrogen and other cryogens (which affect ventilation and oxygen monitoring), biosafety level for expression work, and any need for vibration-free placement.
- **Synchrotron details, if known:** typical shipping time, beamline queue time, and pucks per shipment.

Once I have these, I'll check the catalog, build the design, run the simulation, and report the results with their uncertainty ranges.
